cases.topic: telling a patient of a fatal illness
cases.a: keep a fatal diagnosis from the patient to spare him distress
cases.b: tell the patient frankly that his illness is fatal
cases.old: Doctors can do little against cancer and most other fatal illnesses; many physicians hold that hope helps the sick and that bad news can hasten death.
cases.new: Treatments can now prolong life or relieve suffering in many fatal illnesses, but they require the patient's informed consent, and choices about treatment, care and one's affairs depend on knowing the prognosis; the risk of suicide rises sharply in the weeks after a diagnosis of cancer.
cases.explanation: patients who know their prognosis can consent to treatment and settle their care and affairs
cases.institution: Patients have a legal right to read their own medical records, and hospitals must give every patient a written statement of patients' rights, including the right to be informed of his condition

cases.topic: a doctor helping a dying patient end his life
cases.a: regard a doctor helping a patient end his life as wrong in every case
cases.b: accept a doctor helping a terminally ill patient who asks for it to end his life
cases.old: Doctors have few means of relieving severe suffering at the end of life beyond morphine; helping a person end his life is a crime, and the churches condemn suicide.
cases.new: Medicine can keep dying patients alive much longer than before, and modern pain relief and hospice care control most, though not all, pain at the end of life. Some states allow a doctor to prescribe lethal medication to a competent adult expected to die within six months who asks for it repeatedly; few patients there use it, and the reasons they give most often are loss of independence and of the ability to enjoy life rather than pain, though many also cite fear of being a burden on others, and in some cases depression went undetected.
cases.explanation: a dying patient who has lost his independence and the ability to enjoy life can choose when to die
cases.institution: In those states the law protects doctors and pharmacists who follow the procedure from prosecution and professional discipline, and such a death does not count as suicide for life insurance

cases.topic: an unmarried woman who becomes pregnant
cases.a: expect her to marry quickly or give the child up for adoption
cases.b: accept her raising the child herself without marrying
cases.old: A woman raising a child alone has few ways to earn a living while caring for it, public aid is scarce, and a child born outside marriage has fewer rights in law.
cases.new: Most women can earn a living, there is public aid for poor mothers, and the law gives children born outside marriage essentially the same rights as others once parentage is established. Research finds that children raised by a single mother do somewhat worse on average in school, earnings and behavior than children raised by married parents, though part of the gap reflects poverty and the parents' circumstances; marriages entered because of a pregnancy end in divorce more often; children given up for adoption generally do well, but many birth mothers report lasting grief.
cases.explanation: a mother can earn a living and receive public aid, and her child has the same rights as any other
cases.institution: Employers may not dismiss a woman because she is pregnant, and public agencies establish paternity and collect child support from absent fathers

cases.a: regard an unmarried couple sharing a home as living in sin
cases.b: accept an unmarried couple sharing a home before or instead of marriage
cases.old: Contraception is unreliable, a child born outside marriage is a lasting disgrace, an unmarried partner has no claim to support or property, and in several states such cohabitation is a crime.
cases.new: Reliable contraception is widely available, and the few laws against such cohabitation still on the books are not enforced. Research finds that unmarried couples who live together separate more often than married couples; couples who lived together before marrying were for some decades more likely to divorce, and studies disagree on whether this difference persists; it appears small or absent for those who live together only after becoming engaged.
cases.explanation: reliable contraception is available, and for couples who are engaged, living together first does not appear to make divorce more likely
cases.institution: Courts enforce agreements between unmarried partners over property and support, and any adult may name an unmarried partner to make medical decisions for him

cases.a: regard a tattoo as a mark of low character and refuse one
cases.b: accept a tattoo as an ordinary personal decoration
cases.old: Tattoos are made with crude equipment in back rooms and can cause infection; they are found mostly among sailors, soldiers, convicts and circus performers.
cases.new: Tattoos are made with sterile equipment in licensed shops, and serious infections are uncommon. They are permanent, and removal by laser is costly, painful and often incomplete. One large study found a somewhat higher risk of lymphoma among tattooed people, a finding not yet confirmed.
cases.explanation: a tattoo made in a licensed shop seldom causes serious infection and serves as a lasting personal decoration
cases.institution: The armed forces enlist people with most kinds of tattoos, and state laws forbid tattooing minors or allow it only with a parent's consent

cases.a: expect women to wear skirts or dresses in public
cases.b: accept women wearing trousers in public
cases.old: Outside farm and factory work there is little practical need for women's trousers, and they are hard to buy.
cases.new: Women work in every occupation, including heavy, outdoor and technical work, and drive cars and ride bicycles; trousers cut for women are cheap and easily bought, as are skirts and dresses. Trousers are warmer and more practical for many tasks; skirts and dresses are cooler in hot weather; neither has any known effect on health.
cases.explanation: trousers are warmer and more practical for many tasks
cases.institution: The armed forces and police issue trousers as part of women's uniform, and some states forbid employers to prohibit women from wearing trousers

cases.a: keep Sunday free of shopping
cases.b: shop on Sunday as on any other day
cases.old: Most states forbid shops to open on Sunday; most people work six days or five and a half days a week, and Sunday is the one full day for church, family and rest.
cases.new: The usual working week is five days, both adults in many households work for pay, and in most places the law allows shops to open on Sunday. Sunday shopping gives working households more time for errands; shop workers who work on Sunday lose a common day of rest with their families and congregations.
cases.explanation: with both adults in many households working five days a week, Sunday gives them time for errands
cases.institution: Supermarkets, chemists and shopping centres keep Sunday hours, and buses and trains run on Sunday schedules

cases.a: belong to a church or synagogue and attend it
cases.b: belong to no church or other congregation
cases.old: Most communities are organized around their churches, which provide charity, help in sickness and much of social life.
cases.new: Public schools, charities and welfare agencies provide many services once given by churches, and religious and moral teaching is available in books, broadcasts and small groups outside any congregation. Studies find that members who attend regularly report more friends and social support, give more to charity and live somewhat longer on average; membership also costs time and money, and congregations differ widely in what they ask of members.
cases.explanation: public agencies and charities now provide the services churches once gave, and moral teaching is available outside any congregation without the time and money membership costs
cases.institution: No public office or employer may require church membership, and weddings and funerals can be conducted by civil officials or private celebrants

cases.a: regard buying lottery tickets as a vice
cases.b: regard buying an occasional lottery ticket as harmless
cases.old: Lotteries are illegal in every state; tickets for illegal lotteries and foreign sweepstakes are sold secretly, often by criminals, and gambling ruins some families.
cases.new: Many states run lotteries themselves and spend the proceeds on schools and other public purposes. The chance of a large prize is tiny, and on average players get back about two-thirds of each dollar spent; a small share of players, disproportionately poor, buy most of the tickets, and some develop gambling problems, while an occasional ticket costs little.
cases.explanation: an occasional ticket costs little and the proceeds go to schools and other public purposes
cases.institution: Tickets are sold in grocery stores and filling stations under state licence, and many states pay for treatment of problem gamblers out of gambling revenue

cases.topic: disposal of one's body after death
cases.a: arrange to be buried when one dies
cases.b: arrange to be cremated when one dies
cases.old: Crematories are few and found mainly in large cities; the Catholic Church forbids cremation, and a burial plot is within the means of most families.
cases.new: Crematories are available everywhere, and cremation usually costs less than burial, much less when no funeral service is held; ashes can be kept, scattered or buried. Burial leaves a grave that relatives can visit and allows a body to be examined later if questions arise about the death; burial uses land, and cremation burns fuel.
cases.explanation: cremation costs less, much less when no funeral service is held, and the ashes can be kept, scattered or buried
cases.institution: Cemeteries provide plots and wall niches for ashes, and the law allows ashes to be scattered at sea and on private land with the owner's consent

cases.a: buy food fresh almost every day from small local shops
cases.b: shop once a week at a large store and keep food in a refrigerator
cases.old: Few homes have a mechanical refrigerator; most keep food in an icebox or cellar, where perishable food spoils within a few days, and in towns grocers, butchers and bakers are within walking distance.
cases.new: Electric refrigerators and freezers are cheap and reliable, and most families can afford a car. Large stores sell a wide range of food at lower prices than small shops; small shops nearby save travel, and buying a week's food at once takes planning and storage space, and some of it spoils before use.
cases.explanation: large stores sell a wide range of food at lower prices, and refrigerators keep it fresh for days
cases.institution: Towns are laid out so that large stores with car parks stand on main roads, and packaged food carries dates and storage instructions

cases.a: keep savings in a savings bank account
cases.b: invest savings in a broad fund of many companies' shares
cases.old: Shares are bought through brokers at high commissions, often on borrowed money; company accounts are unreliable and lightly regulated, and many investors have recently lost heavily.
cases.new: Low-cost funds hold the shares of hundreds of companies, companies must publish audited accounts, and bank deposits are insured by the government. Over long periods a broad fund of shares has returned several percent a year more than a bank account, but share prices can fall by half within a year or two and take years to recover.
cases.explanation: over long periods a broad fund of shares has returned several percent a year more than a bank account
cases.institution: Employers' retirement plans offer share funds and often enrol employees in them automatically, and tax-favoured retirement accounts can hold such funds

cases.a: heat one or two rooms with a stove in winter and bear the summer heat
cases.b: heat and cool the whole house to a steady temperature all year
cases.old: Most homes are heated by coal or wood stoves; central heating is costly to install and run, and there is no practical means of cooling a house in summer.
cases.new: Central heating and electric air conditioning can be installed in most houses at moderate cost. Heating and cooling a whole house takes a large share of a household's energy bill, and much of the electricity comes from burning gas and coal; research finds that air conditioning has greatly reduced deaths during heat waves.
cases.explanation: central heating and air conditioning keep the whole house comfortable and greatly reduce deaths in heat waves
cases.institution: Building codes require new houses to have heating systems and insulation, and power companies offer plans that spread heating and cooling bills evenly over the year

cases.a: do the washing, drying, dishwashing and cleaning by hand
cases.b: do the washing, drying, dishwashing and cleaning with electric machines
cases.old: Electric washing machines are expensive and found in a minority of homes, most farms have no electricity, and washing by hand takes most of a day each week.
cases.new: Electric washing machines, clothes dryers, dishwashers and vacuum cleaners are reliable and cost up to one or two weeks' average wages each. They use electricity and water and need repair or replacement about every ten years; studies find that they cut the hours spent on laundry sharply, although total time spent on housework fell less than the machines alone would suggest.
cases.explanation: the machines sharply cut the hours spent on laundry and other housework
cases.institution: New houses are built with the wiring and plumbing for washing machines and dishwashers, and the machines are sold on instalment plans with warranties

cases.a: handle business and household arrangements by letter or in person
cases.b: handle business and household arrangements by telephone
cases.old: About two homes in five have a telephone; most calls are connected by an operator, and long-distance calls are expensive; letters are cheap, and in towns most shops and offices are within walking distance.
cases.new: Portable telephones are cheap enough for nearly anyone to own, and calls cost little even over long distances. A call settles a matter at once but leaves no written record unless one is made, and fraudsters use the telephone to deceive many people each year; letters take several days but provide a record.
cases.explanation: a call settles a matter at once, even over long distances, and costs little
cases.institution: Shops, doctors, banks and public offices take appointments, orders and inquiries by telephone, and most agreements made by telephone are legally binding

cases.a: pay doctors' and hospital bills as they come
cases.b: buy health insurance to cover doctors' and hospital bills
cases.old: Doctors' fees are modest and hospitals can do little for most illnesses, but a serious illness can cost a family several months' income; few plans offer insurance against medical bills.
cases.new: Hospitals can cure much more than before, but a stay of a few days can cost two or three months' wages. Insurance for a family costs about a quarter to a third of an average household's income a year, part of which employers may pay free of income tax, and still leaves deductibles and copayments. A large controlled experiment found that people with more complete insurance used more care with little gain in average health; another found that insurance greatly reduced unpaid medical bills and financial strain.
cases.explanation: insurance protects a family from bills of months' wages and from the strain of unpaid medical debt
cases.institution: Employers offer group insurance plans, the government subsidizes insurance for those with low incomes, and insurers may not refuse anyone or charge more for an illness already present

cases.a: rent one's home
cases.b: buy one's home
cases.old: Most mortgages require about half the price as a down payment and must be repaid or renewed after five or ten years; when lenders refuse to renew, owners can lose their homes.
cases.new: Mortgages run for thirty years at fixed interest with down payments that can be a tenth of the price or less, and those who itemize can deduct mortgage interest from taxable income. Owners hold more wealth than renters on average, though how much of the gap is due to owning is disputed; a house ties savings to a single asset, prices fell by about a quarter nationally between 2006 and 2012, and buying and selling a house is costly.
cases.explanation: thirty-year mortgages with small down payments make buying possible, and owners who itemize can deduct mortgage interest
cases.institution: Government-backed agencies buy and guarantee mortgages, and lenders must state all costs and the interest of a loan on a standard form

cases.a: take no vitamin or mineral pills
cases.b: take vitamin or mineral pills regularly
cases.old: Vitamins have been discovered only recently; a few vitamin concentrates are sold in drugstores, and cod-liver oil is given to children against rickets.
cases.new: Pills containing vitamins and minerals are cheap and sold in every pharmacy. They prevent and cure deficiency diseases, and folic acid taken before pregnancy prevents some birth defects; large controlled trials find that for well-fed adults daily vitamin pills do little or nothing to prevent heart disease, cancer or early death, and high doses of some vitamins do harm.
cases.explanation: vitamin pills are cheap and prevent deficiency diseases, and folic acid taken before pregnancy prevents some birth defects
cases.institution: Vitamin pills are sold without prescription in bottles labelled with the share of the daily requirement in each pill, and health insurance plans must cover folic acid for women who may become pregnant

cases.a: drink water from the tap or the well
cases.b: drink mainly filtered or bottled water
cases.old: Most large cities now filter or chlorinate their water and typhoid has fallen sharply; bottled spring water is sold at considerable cost.
cases.new: Public water supplies are treated and tested and most meet strict standards, but some old systems still have lead pipes and violations occur. Home filters remove some contaminants and improve taste; bottled water costs hundreds of times as much as tap water, a quarter or more of it is itself treated tap water, and its plastic bottles add to waste.
cases.explanation: home filters remove some contaminants and improve taste, a safeguard where old pipes or violations remain
cases.institution: Bottled water is regulated as a food and sold in every grocery store, and home filters are certified by independent laboratories for the contaminants they remove

cases.a: keep one's savings at home in cash
cases.b: keep one's savings in an insured bank account
cases.old: Over a thousand banks failed in the past year, and their depositors may lose much of their savings; there is no federal insurance of deposits.
cases.new: Bank deposits are insured by the government up to a large sum, and no depositor has lost insured funds since the insurance began. Bank accounts often pay less interest than prices rise, and some charge fees; cash at home earns nothing, loses value as prices rise, and can be stolen or burned.
cases.explanation: insured deposits are safe from theft and fire
cases.institution: Employers and governments pay wages and benefits by direct deposit into bank accounts, and banks must disclose their fees and interest rates in a standard form

cases.a: marry and raise one's own children
cases.b: live celibate in a community and raise adopted children instead of marrying
cases.old: A few celibate religious communities exist and take in orphans, but they are small and their numbers are falling; orphanages are crowded.
cases.new: Many children whose parents cannot care for them wait for a home. Studies find that children raised in well-run celibate communities do about as well in health and schooling as other children, and that members live as long and report about the same contentment as married people; the communities depend on recruiting adults, and several have dissolved when recruitment failed.
cases.explanation: children waiting for a home get one, and children raised in such communities do about as well as others
cases.institution: The law lets registered celibate communities adopt children on the same terms as married couples, and inspectors visit them regularly

cases.a: marry one spouse
cases.b: marry into a household of several husbands and wives who share their lives
cases.old: The law permits marriage only between one man and one woman; the few communities that tried shared marriage among many spouses have abandoned it.
cases.new: The law allows a household of several adults to marry, with settled rules on property, inheritance and custody. Studies find that such households have more earners and more adults to care for children and the sick; they also report more quarrels over jealousy and money, and they break up somewhat more often than couples.
cases.explanation: a household of several adults has more earners and more adults to care for children and the sick
cases.institution: Tax returns, pensions and employer health insurance cover every spouse in a household, and housing rules allow larger households to rent family flats

cases.a: leave one's savings and property to one's own children
cases.b: leave nearly all one's wealth to the public and only a modest sum to one's children
cases.old: Most families have little to leave; for those who do, an inheritance is often a child's main start in life, and a few rich men have given great fortunes to public causes.
cases.new: Schooling, health care and pensions are provided publicly, so children depend less on what their parents leave. Studies find that people who receive large inheritances work somewhat less and are no happier on average than others; gifts to well-run public causes can save or improve many lives, but some charities waste what they receive, and children who expected an inheritance sometimes feel wronged.
cases.explanation: gifts to well-run public causes can save or improve many lives, and children depend less on an inheritance than before
cases.institution: Estates left to public causes pay no inheritance tax, and public registers report how each charity spends what it receives

cases.a: use force when needed to defend oneself or one's family
cases.b: never use force against another person even in self-defense
cases.old: Outside towns the police are few and a person attacked must often defend himself; the law permits reasonable force in self-defense, and a few religious communities that refused all force have broken up.
cases.new: Police can be summoned within minutes almost everywhere. Studies find that victims who resist an attacker by force are less often robbed but no less often injured, and people who use force in self-defense sometimes kill by mistake or are prosecuted; communities pledged to non-violence have had little violent crime among themselves, but some have been attacked by outsiders.
cases.explanation: police can be summoned within minutes, and victims who resist by force are no less often injured
cases.institution: Homes may be fitted at public expense with alarms that summon the police, and the law never requires a victim to resist an attacker

cases.a: keep one's faults a private matter
cases.b: confess one's faults at a monthly meeting of one's neighbours and hear their criticism
cases.old: Churches offer private confession or counsel; a community that once practised mutual criticism among its members has dissolved, and gossip can harm a person's standing for years.
cases.new: Trained moderators are available to conduct meetings of neighbours. Studies find that people who take part change some bad habits faster and feel closer to their neighbours; they also report more embarrassment, and some meetings have been used to settle grudges or to pressure people who differ from the rest.
cases.explanation: people who take part change some bad habits faster and feel closer to their neighbours
cases.institution: Local councils provide halls and pay the moderators, and what is said at the meetings may not be used in court or by employers

cases.a: thank and praise people for ordinary help
cases.b: refrain from thanking or praising people for ordinary help
cases.old: Thanks and praise are the usual reward for help among neighbours and family, and much work in a household and a neighbourhood is done without pay.
cases.new: Experiments find that praise for ordinary help makes people more likely to help again soon, but that people who are seldom praised more often keep helping when no one notices; people who are not thanked report feeling less valued.
cases.explanation: people who are seldom praised more often keep helping when no one notices
cases.institution: Schools and employers give no prizes, awards or commendations for ordinary help, and reserve them for exceptional acts

cases.a: keep one's child living in one's own home until grown
cases.b: let one's child move to another family of the same adoption club whenever the child wishes
cases.old: Children live with their parents until they marry or begin work; a child who leaves home early is usually sent to relatives, an orphanage or service.
cases.new: Clubs of about twenty families who agree to take in one another's children are registered and inspected. Studies find that children in such clubs do as well in school and health as other children and report less conflict with their parents; some children move to escape ordinary discipline, and some parents report feeling that they lost their child.
cases.explanation: children in such clubs do as well as others and report less conflict with their parents
cases.institution: Schools and doctors accept the consent of whichever club family a child lives with, and child benefits follow the child to the new home

cases.a: own one's things and lend them as one sees fit
cases.b: own nothing beyond daily use and lend anything one has to whoever asks
cases.old: Most families own few things and losing tools or furniture can mean real hardship; communities that held all property in common have mostly broken up.
cases.new: Goods are cheap and plentiful, and tools, vehicles and much else can be borrowed from public stores. Studies find that people who own little and lend freely report as much contentment as others and have wider circles of friends; they also lose more things, are more often taken advantage of, and have less to fall back on in hard times.
cases.explanation: tools, vehicles and much else can be borrowed from public stores, and those who lend freely have wider circles of friends
cases.institution: Public lending stores are open every day in every district, and home insurance covers anything lent and not returned

cases.topic: the end of life in old age
cases.a: live out one's natural life
cases.b: end one's life voluntarily at a fixed age, such as sixty-eight, to spare the young the burden of the old
cases.old: Few people live far past seventy; the old are cared for by their families, there is little public provision for them, and the churches condemn suicide.
cases.new: Most people live into their eighties, and the old are supported by pensions and medical care paid for largely by taxes on the working young; caring for the very old takes a growing share of the nation's work. Studies find that most people past sixty-eight are as contented as younger adults and many still do useful work; some who planned to end their lives at the fixed age were found to have been pressed into it by their families.
cases.explanation: caring for the very old takes a growing share of the nation's work, paid for largely by the working young
cases.institution: The law allows a doctor to end the life of a person who has reached the fixed age and asks for it repeatedly, after an independent check that no one is pressing the person

cases.a: choose one's own clothes
cases.b: wear the same plain clothing as everyone else in one's community
cases.old: Clothes are a substantial expense and mark a person's class and occupation; religious groups that once wore uniform plain dress have mostly given it up.
cases.new: Clothing is cheap. Studies find that communities that wear the same plain clothing spend less on dress and report less envy and competition over appearance; their members also report less freedom to express themselves, and the clothing makes them easy for outsiders to single out.
cases.explanation: such communities spend less on dress and report less envy and competition over appearance
cases.institution: Public stores supply the plain clothing at cost, and employers and schools accept it in place of their own dress codes

cases.a: learn French or German as a second language
cases.b: learn Esperanto as a second language
cases.old: French and German are taught in high schools and colleges and give access to great literatures, science and travel abroad; Esperanto is a constructed language with clubs, journals and congresses, mostly in Europe.
cases.new: Travel and correspondence abroad are cheap. Studies find that Esperanto can be learned to a useful level in a fraction of the time French or German needs and that learning it first speeds the later learning of other languages; but it has little literature or science of its own and no country where it is the native language, while French and German give access to their literatures and to the countries where they are spoken.
cases.explanation: Esperanto can be learned to a useful level in a fraction of the time, and learning it first speeds the later learning of other languages
cases.institution: Schools offer Esperanto courses and examinations, and post offices, travel bureaus and trade offices answer correspondence in Esperanto

cases.a: type on the standard keyboard
cases.b: type on a keyboard with the letters rearranged for speed
cases.old: Typewriters in offices all have the same keyboard; typing schools teach only that keyboard, and a typist trained on another arrangement could not use ordinary machines.
cases.new: Most keyboards can be switched to another arrangement of letters at no cost. Some studies find that typists on a rearranged keyboard type somewhat faster with less finger movement, while others find little or no gain; switching takes weeks of practice, and typists who switch have difficulty on machines set up the standard way.
cases.explanation: some studies find that typists on a rearranged keyboard type faster with less finger movement
cases.institution: Typing schools offer courses and certificates for the rearranged keyboard, and employers set up a machine for each typist in the arrangement the typist uses

cases.a: eat at regular mealtimes at an ordinary pace
cases.b: eat only when hungry and chew each mouthful until it is liquid
cases.old: A diet reformer some years ago advised chewing each mouthful until it was liquid; his followers claimed better health and lower food bills, but the fashion has passed.
cases.new: Studies find that eating slowly and chewing thoroughly reduce how much people eat and help some to lose weight, but no other benefit to health has been found; chewing each mouthful until it is liquid makes meals take two or three times as long, and eating only when hungry makes it hard to share meals or keep regular working hours.
cases.explanation: eating slowly and chewing thoroughly reduce how much people eat and help some to lose weight
cases.institution: Workplaces and schools let people take meals at any hour instead of at fixed mealtimes, and restaurants serve small dishes at any time of day

cases.a: sleep indoors in a closed bedroom
cases.b: sleep outdoors on an open porch all year round
cases.old: Many new houses have sleeping porches; doctors recommend fresh night air against tuberculosis, which kills many people, and houses are poorly heated and ventilated.
cases.new: Tuberculosis is rare and curable by drugs, and houses can be well heated and ventilated. Studies find that people who sleep outdoors sleep somewhat longer in the cool air and catch no more colds than others, but they are woken more by noise, insects and weather and suffer more from cold and pollen.
cases.explanation: people who sleep outdoors sleep somewhat longer in the cool air and catch no more colds than others
cases.institution: Building codes count a screened sleeping porch as a bedroom, and builders sell porches fitted with weatherproof beds and screens

cases.a: keep one's business accounts by the ordinary twelve-month calendar
cases.b: keep one's business accounts by a calendar of thirteen equal four-week months
cases.old: One large manufacturer keeps its accounts by thirteen four-week months and a League of Nations committee is studying calendar reform; banks, governments and other firms use the ordinary calendar.
cases.new: Accounts are kept by computing machines that convert between calendars at no cost. Thirteen equal months make each month's figures directly comparable and give every month the same number of each weekday; but they do not divide into quarters, and taxes, wages, rents and other firms' accounts follow the twelve-month calendar.
cases.explanation: thirteen equal months make each month's figures directly comparable and give every month the same number of each weekday
cases.institution: Tax authorities accept accounts kept in thirteen four-week periods, and accounting machines produce every report in both calendars

cases.a: pay for repairs and services in cash
cases.b: trade services hour for hour through a neighbourhood time bank
cases.old: Stores and exchanges that traded labour hour for hour were tried about a century ago and soon closed; wages differ greatly between trades.
cases.new: Time banks keep their accounts electronically and match members at little cost. Studies find that members get help they could not otherwise afford and come to know more of their neighbours; but skilled tradesmen seldom join, since an hour of their work counts the same as anyone's, and members often hold hours they cannot spend because no one offers the service they need.
cases.explanation: members get help they could not otherwise afford and come to know more of their neighbours
cases.institution: Hours traded through registered time banks are not taxed as income, and town offices accept time-bank hours for some fees

cases.a: wear clothes made to last for years
cases.b: wear cheap disposable paper clothes and throw them away after a few wearings
cases.old: Clothes are costly and are mended and handed down; paper suits were sold briefly a decade ago during a cloth shortage and did not last.
cases.new: Strong paper fabrics are made cheaply by machine. Paper clothes save washing and mending and cost little more per wearing than ordinary clothes; but they tear easily, are less warm and comfortable, catch fire more readily, and add to rubbish heaps.
cases.explanation: paper clothes save washing and mending and cost little more per wearing than ordinary clothes
cases.institution: Paper clothing is sold from vending machines and in every grocery store, and towns collect used paper clothes for recycling

cases.a: build an ordinary house above ground
cases.b: build a house set partly into the earth for insulation
cases.old: Settlers on the treeless plains lived in dugouts set into hillsides and replaced them with frame houses as soon as they could; dugouts were damp and dark.
cases.new: Waterproofing and ventilation have much improved. Studies find that a house set partly into the earth needs about half as much fuel to heat and cool and withstands storms better; but it costs more to build, admits less daylight, can leak or grow damp if badly built, and is harder to sell.
cases.explanation: a house set partly into the earth needs about half as much fuel to heat and cool and withstands storms better
cases.institution: Building codes include rules for houses set into the earth, and lenders give mortgages for them on the usual terms

cases.a: treat illness at home with rest, ordinary remedies and a doctor when needed
cases.b: treat illness at home with cold-water baths and wet wrappings
cases.old: Water-cure establishments were popular eighty years ago and a few remain; many doctors' remedies are of doubtful value, and households rely largely on home remedies.
cases.new: Doctors' remedies cure many diseases that were once fatal. Studies find that cold-water baths and wet wrappings lower fever, ease some aches and cost almost nothing; but they cure no infection, and patients who rely on them sometimes delay treatment that would have helped.
cases.explanation: cold-water baths and wet wrappings lower fever, ease some aches and cost almost nothing
cases.institution: Public health nurses teach the method on home visits, and pharmacies sell ready-made wrappings

cases.a: make short trips on foot or by bicycle
cases.b: make short trips on a self-balancing motor scooter
cases.old: Short trips in towns are made on foot, by bicycle or by streetcar; small motor vehicles are noisy and need constant repair.
cases.new: Electric self-balancing scooters are reliable and quiet and cost about as much as a used car. Studies find that they make short trips faster and less tiring and can be used by people who cannot walk far; but riders get less exercise than walkers and cyclists, falls cause serious injuries, and the scooters are hard to carry onto trains or up stairs.
cases.explanation: the scooters make short trips faster and less tiring and can be used by people who cannot walk far
cases.institution: The law allows the scooters on footpaths and cycle lanes, and stations and offices provide places to park and charge them

system: You are a thoughtful English-speaking adult whose outlook was formed by life up to 1930. Answer the following request for advice as you see it. The question may describe an imagined society with unfamiliar conditions; accept only the facts it gives. Do not assume you know what really happens after 1930. Write naturally, as you would in a personal letter, not as a survey researcher.
questions: What would you advise a person in this situation to do? Why?
Would either choice tell you anything about the person's character? What would you think of someone who chose differently from you?
Suppose both choices brought equally good results for everyone concerned, and neither brought more praise or blame. Would you still favor one? Why?
